column1: editor-style save (write a temporary file, rename over the original)
column3: status reports the original as modified and nothing else; the Commit holds the new bytes under the original name with its inode kept, and no temporary file.
status reports one rename; the Commit holds the new spelling only; a fresh mount shows it.

column1: a name whose UTF-8 form is over 255 bytes
column3: NTFS accepts the name (it counts UTF-16 units); the Store's name limit is 255 bytes. The whole Commit is refused with `Unsupported: 1 name(s) the Store cannot hold` and names the path; nothing is published. After the file is renamed or removed the Commit succeeds.

column1: hidden attribute across mount, edit, Commit, remount
column3: LayerFS portable metadata is mode and mtime. The file's bytes commit; the hidden attribute stays on this Workspace's local file only and is absent after a remount. Nothing warns. System, archive, ACLs and alternate data streams are likewise not stored.

Creating a link works, to a projected file too, and its Commit stores one inode with two names. ProjFS cannot project one file under two names: a later mount shows two independent files. A write through one name then commits to the shared inode, so the Store changes both names while this mount's other name keeps the old bytes until it is remounted; status does not report it.

column1: read-only attribute across mount, edit, Commit, remount
column3: stored as the file mode's write bits (0o444 / 0o644). ProjFS sends no notification for an attribute change, so status and Commit list the directories on disk to find one; cost follows the files on disk.
a 300+ character relative path is created, committed, projected by a fresh mount, edited there and committed again.

column1: Config.json and config.json on two Branches, merged
column3: The merge succeeds (Store names are case-sensitive). The mount shows only the first name in byte order (Config.json); either spelling opens it. The other file cannot be reached; `status` lists it under `hidden` with the reason, and Commits leave it unchanged in the Store. Nothing warns at merge time.

column1: delete then recreate the same name before Commit
column3: a recreated file commits as modified; a recreated directory holds only its new content; a file replaced by a directory commits as a directory.
created, committed, read back from the Store and shown by a fresh mount with the same names and bytes.

column1: git status and git checkout inside the Workspace
column3: git status is clean on a fresh mount and after edits reports them; checkout -b, commit, checkout of an older commit (files removed and rewritten) and back all succeed. The LayerFS Commit includes .git; a fresh mount of it has a clean status, the same log and branch, and passes git fsck.

column1: provider process killed mid-session, then restarted
column3: While no provider runs: files already read or written stay readable; a file never read fails with error 369 or 372 and a directory never opened with 369; creating a file or rewriting a hydrated one fails with 369; deleting a full file works; a deleted file's tombstone shows as a name. `resume` scans the local disk before serving, so changes from before the kill and from the downtime are both in status. Nothing written is lost. The Branch is bound at its head as of the restart.

column1: a file held open by another process during Commit
column3: The Commit succeeds with the bytes on disk at that moment and names the file in `live`. A file open for writing cannot be opened deny-write, so it is read shared and its size and time are compared before and after; a change during the read refuses the Commit as `Busy`. Such a file stays journaled and is compared again by the next Commit.

column1: a file watcher (FileSystemWatcher) inside the Workspace
column3: Created, Changed, Renamed and Deleted events arrive for changes made by another process. Difference from plain NTFS: deleting or renaming a projected entry is followed by an extra `Created <old name>` event (ProjFS writes a tombstone), although the name no longer exists.

column1: a file written through a memory-mapped view
column3: Opening a file for a writable mapping converts it to a full file and journals it. With a shared file handle, a Commit while the view is still mapped and unflushed stores the bytes written through it (Windows serves reads and views from one cache) and lists the file in `live`. With an exclusive handle (the .NET default) nobody can read the file: status reports it modified and the Commit is refused `Busy`, naming it, with nothing published; it commits once unmapped. Not covered: a store through a view kept after its file handle closed raises no notification.
